title: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
summary: How a GPU kernel launch becomes a grid of blocks of threads, how threads find their data, why warps of 32 diverge, how blocks cooperate and sync, what limits occupancy, and how Metal names the same ideas.
outcomes: Compute a thread's global index and the block count for any N with ceiling division, and explain why the bounds check is needed
Explain how blocks split into warps of 32 and predict which branches make a warp diverge
Use shared memory and __syncthreads correctly, and explain why blocks cannot wait on each other except within a cluster
Compute SM occupancy from registers, shared memory and per-SM limits
Translate CUDA grids, blocks, warps and barriers into Metal threadgroups, SIMD-groups and dispatch calls

lessons.title: One kernel, many threads: grids, blocks and SMs

blocks.md:
On a CPU you add two vectors with a loop: one thread walks `i` from 0 to `n-1`. A GPU has tens to hundreds of **Streaming Multiprocessors** (SMs), each able to keep hundreds of threads in flight, so a single loop would use a tiny sliver of the chip.

CUDA turns the loop inside out. You write the *body* once as a **kernel** (a function marked `__global__`), and a **kernel launch** starts many threads that all run that same body. Each thread asks "which element am I?" and does just that one.

The CPU side is the **host** and the GPU side is the **device**. Applications always start on the host; the host allocates device memory, launches kernels and waits for them. A launch is *asynchronous*: the host call returns before the kernel finishes (or even starts), so you must synchronize, for example with `cudaDeviceSynchronize()`, before reading results.

Threads come in a fixed hierarchy:

- A **thread block** is a group of threads that run together on *one* SM and can share that SM's fast on-chip **shared memory**. On current GPUs a block holds at most 1024 threads.
- A **grid** is all the blocks of one launch. Every block in a grid has the same size and shape.
- Grids and blocks can be 1, 2 or 3 dimensional, which is purely a convenience for mapping threads onto arrays and images.

The launch syntax `kernel<<<blocks, threadsPerBlock>>>(args)` is called the **execution configuration**.

blocks.caption: The CUDA Programming Guide's running example: 4 thread blocks of 256 threads add two 1024-element vectors.

blocks.title: From a kernel launch to blocks on SMs

scenes.caption: The host launches vecAdd with an execution configuration of 4 blocks of 256 threads. The call returns to the CPU right away.
The launch creates a grid of 4 identical thread blocks, 1024 threads in total. Every thread will run the same kernel body.
Each whole block is placed on one SM, where its threads share registers and shared memory. Which SM gets which block, and when, is up to the hardware.

blocks.md: That last point is the key design decision. A grid may hold millions of blocks while the GPU has only tens or hundreds of SMs, so blocks are queued and handed to SMs as space frees up. CUDA gives **no guarantee about the order** in which blocks run or which SM they land on. In exchange, the same program runs on a GPU with one SM or thousands.

blocks.title: The same 8-block grid on a 2-SM and a 4-SM GPU

scenes.caption: Simplified: each block takes one time unit and an SM runs one block at a time (real SMs keep several blocks resident). With 2 SMs the grid needs 4 waves.
The unchanged program on a GPU with 4 SMs finishes in 2 waves. Blocks are independent, so the hardware is free to spread them out.
The order is not guaranteed either: here block 5 runs first and block 4 last. A correct kernel must give the same answer for any placement and order.

blocks.md: Blocks must not depend on each other. A thread may not wait for, or read results produced by, a thread in a different block of the same grid, because that block may not have been scheduled yet. (Thread block clusters, in lesson 4, are the one opt-in exception.)

blocks.question: Block 0 of a kernel spins in a loop waiting for a flag that block 1 sets. On a big GPU it works; on a small GPU it hangs. Why?
options: The small GPU has a smaller warp size, so the flag write is lost
Blocks may run in any order and need not be resident together; if block 0 occupies the only free slot, block 1 never starts
Global memory is not visible across blocks until the kernel ends, on any GPU
The small GPU runs blocks in reverse order, so block 1 always finishes first
blocks.explain: CUDA promises nothing about block scheduling order or co-residency. On a GPU with spare SMs both blocks happen to run at once; when resources are tight, block 0 can sit on the SM forever while block 1 waits in the queue. Correct code never makes one block wait on another.

blocks.question: A, B and C are allocated with cudaMallocManaged (unified memory, readable by host and device). The host launches `vecAdd<<<4, 256>>>(A, B, C)` and on the very next line prints `C[0]`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: a kernel launch blocks until the kernel finishes
The launch is asynchronous, so the host may read C before the kernel has written it; call cudaDeviceSynchronize() first
Only block 0 has finished by then, but C[0] belongs to block 0 so it is fine
Unified memory cannot be read by the host after a launch
blocks.explain: The guide states that kernel launches are asynchronous with respect to the host thread: the kernel may not have finished, or even started. Its unified memory example calls cudaDeviceSynchronize() before the host touches the results. Blocks also have no guaranteed order, so 'block 0 finishes first' is not a safe assumption either.

lessons.title: Computing a thread's global index: vector add end to end

blocks.md:
Inside a kernel every thread can read four built-in variables, each a 3-component vector with `.x`, `.y`, `.z`:

- `threadIdx`: this thread's index inside its block, from 0 to `blockDim.x - 1`.
- `blockIdx`: this block's index inside the grid, from 0 to `gridDim.x - 1`.
- `blockDim`: the block size from the launch.
- `gridDim`: the grid size from the launch.

Dimensions you do not specify default to 1. The values differ per thread only for `threadIdx` and `blockIdx`.

blocks.caption: The global index for a 1D launch: skip the threads of all earlier blocks, then add your position inside your own block.

blocks.md:
With `vecAdd<<<4, 256>>>`, block 0 covers elements 0 to 255, block 1 starts at 256, block 2 at 512 and block 3 at 768. Thread 37 of block 1 handles element $1 \times 256 + 37 = 293$.

Real sizes rarely divide evenly. To cover $N$ elements with blocks of $b$ threads you need the **ceiling** of $N/b$ blocks, which integer code writes as `(N + b - 1) / b` (or `cuda::ceil_div(N, b)`).

blocks.caption: Adding b - 1 before the integer division rounds up, adding one more block only when there is a remainder.

blocks.prompt: You need to add two vectors of N = 10 elements using blocks of 4 threads. How many blocks do you launch, how many threads run, and what must the kernel do about the extras?
blocks.reveal: $\lceil 10/4 \rceil = 3$ blocks, so 12 threads run for 10 elements. Threads with global index 10 and 11 would read and write past the end of the arrays, so the kernel must check `if (i < N)` and let those threads do nothing.

blocks.title: N = 10, 4 threads per block: who computes what

scenes.caption: 3 blocks of 4 threads: 12 threads, each with a (blockIdx.x, threadIdx.x) pair. No thread knows its element yet.
Each thread computes i = blockIdx.x x 4 + threadIdx.x. Block 1 starts at 4 and block 2 at 8, so the 12 threads get the distinct indices 0 to 11.
The bounds check: threads with i < 10 are active, threads 10 and 11 (the last two of block 2) fail i < N and exit without touching memory.
Active threads write C[i] = A[i] + B[i] in parallel, with A = 3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6,5,3 and B = 2,7,1,8,2,8,1,8,2,8. Two of the 12 threads did no work.

blocks.title: Two threads of vecAdd with N = 1000 and 256-thread blocks

scenes.caption: Host side: (1000 + 255) / 256 = 4 blocks, so 1024 threads launch for 1000 elements.
Thread 231 of block 3: i = 231 + 256 x 3 = 999, the last valid element.
999 < 1000, so this thread performs the add for element 999.
Thread 232 of block 3: i = 232 + 768 = 1000. The check fails and the thread exits. Block 3 has 232 active threads and 24 idle ones.

blocks.md: Launching a few extra threads is cheap; the bounds check is what makes it safe. The guide warns against launching whole blocks in which no thread does useful work.

**Two and three dimensions.** For an image or matrix, launch 2D blocks and a 2D grid with `dim3`, and compute a column and a row with the same formula per axis: `col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x`, `row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y`. The guide's `MatAdd` example uses `dim3 grid(16,16)` and `dim3 block(8,8)`: a 128 by 128 thread layout, 16,384 threads.

Inside a block the threads are linearized with **x fastest**, then y, then z: the linear thread id is `threadIdx.x + threadIdx.y * blockDim.x + threadIdx.z * blockDim.x * blockDim.y`. That linear id decides which warp a thread joins (next lesson).

blocks.title: An 8 x 8 thread layout: 2 x 2 blocks of 4 x 4 threads

scenes.caption: Each cell is one thread, colored by its block's linear id (blockIdx.x + 2 x blockIdx.y). The grid is gridDim = (2, 2) and each block is blockDim = (4, 4).
The thread with blockIdx = (1, 0) and threadIdx = (2, 3): col = 1 x 4 + 2 = 6 and row = 0 x 4 + 3 = 3.
Values now show the row-major element index row x 8 + col. The highlighted thread handles element 3 x 8 + 6 = 30 of the 8 x 8 matrix.

blocks.question: A kernel uses `int i = threadIdx.x + blockDim.x * blockIdx.x;` and is launched with 4,000 blocks of 256 threads on an array of 1,000,000 floats, with no bounds check. What happens?
options: Fine: 4,000 x 256 is close enough to one million
Threads with i from 1,000,000 to 1,023,999 access memory past the end of the arrays
Only the first 3,907 blocks run; the runtime drops the rest automatically
The compiler inserts the bounds check because N is known
blocks.explain: 4,000 x 256 = 1,024,000 threads, so 24,000 threads have an index at or beyond N. Only 3907 blocks were needed (ceil of 1,000,000 / 256), and even then the last block would have 192 idle threads that need the `if (i < N)` check. Nothing drops blocks or adds checks for you.

blocks.question: In a 2D launch with blockDim = (16, 16), which pair of threads in the same block are neighbors in the linear thread order?
options: threadIdx (3, 5) and (3, 6)
threadIdx (3, 5) and (5, 3)
No pair: 2D blocks have no linear order
threadIdx (3, 5) and (4, 5)
blocks.explain: x moves fastest. (3, 5) has linear id 3 + 5 x 16 = 83 and (4, 5) has 84. Moving one step in y jumps by blockDim.x = 16.

lessons.title: Warps and SIMT: 32 threads, one instruction, and divergence

blocks.md:
A thread is the unit you program, but it is not the unit the hardware schedules. Inside an SM each block is split into **warps** of 32 threads. A **warp scheduler** picks a warp that is ready and issues its next instruction to all of its threads at once.

The split is deterministic: warp 0 holds linear thread ids 0 to 31, warp 1 holds 32 to 63, and so on. Inside a warp each thread has a **lane** number from 0 to 31.

blocks.caption: T is the number of threads per block; the CUDA guide gives this rule with warp size 32.

blocks.prompt: You launch blocks of 100 threads. How many warps does each block occupy, and how busy is the last one?
blocks.reveal: $\lceil 100/32 \rceil = 4$ warps. The last warp contains only 4 real threads; its other 28 lanes stay inactive for the whole kernel but still occupy a warp slot. That is why the guide recommends block sizes that are a multiple of 32.

blocks.md:
NVIDIA calls this execution style **SIMT** (single instruction, multiple threads). Each thread has its own registers and its own logical program counter, so the code reads like ordinary scalar C++. But a warp executes **one common instruction at a time**. Full efficiency needs all 32 threads to agree on the path.

If a data-dependent `if` sends some lanes one way and some the other, the warp **diverges**: it runs each taken path in turn, with the lanes that are not on that path masked off. Divergence happens only *within* a warp; different warps run independently.

blocks.title: Active lanes of one warp (lanes 0 to 31, 8 per row)

scenes.caption: Straight-line code: all 32 lanes are active (1) and every issued instruction does 32 threads' worth of work.
`if (threadIdx.x % 2 == 0) { pathA(); }`: while pathA runs, only the 16 even lanes are active. The odd lanes are masked off (0) but the warp still spends the issue slots.
`else { pathB(); }`: now the warp runs pathB with only the 16 odd lanes. Both paths were executed by the warp, each at half utilization.
A block of 100 threads: its last warp has only 4 real threads, so lanes 4 to 31 are inactive for the entire kernel.

blocks.title: Divergent vs warp-aligned branches (simplified cost model)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: pathA is 10 instructions, pathB is 20, one instruction issued per step. With the condition x % 2, every warp contains both even and odd lanes.
So every warp runs both paths back to back: 10 + 20 = 30 instruction steps, half the lanes idle throughout.
Same work, condition (x / 32) % 2: the branch now splits along warp boundaries. Warp 0 runs only pathA (10 steps), warp 1 only pathB (20 steps), all 32 lanes busy. No warp diverges.

blocks.md: The Best Practices Guide gives exactly this advice: when the condition depends on the thread id, write it so it lines up with warps, for example a condition on `threadIdx.x / 32`. For very short branches the compiler may instead use **predication**: it issues both sides and a per-thread predicate decides which threads write results, so small divergent `if`s are often cheap.

SIMT is not the same as SIMD. In CPU SIMD the software sees the vector width and manages lanes itself. In SIMT you write scalar per-thread code and the hardware groups it. Correctness never depends on warps; performance does, much like cache lines.

**Independent thread scheduling.** Before compute capability 7.0 (Volta), a warp shared one program counter plus an active mask, so threads in different branches of the same warp could not wait on each other, and spin locks inside a warp could deadlock. From 7.0 on, the GPU keeps a program counter and call stack *per thread* and can interleave diverged paths, so threads can diverge and reconverge at sub-warp granularity.

The flip side: old **warp-synchronous** code that assumed the 32 lanes always move in lockstep (for example a reduction through shared memory with no synchronization) is no longer safe. Use `__syncwarp()` to make the lanes reconverge and to order their memory accesses.

blocks.caption: A warp-level tree reduction written for independent thread scheduling: every step is fenced with __syncwarp() instead of assuming lockstep.

blocks.question: A block of 256 threads executes `if (threadIdx.x < 96) heavy(); else light();`. How many of its 8 warps diverge on this branch?
options: 0: 96 is a multiple of 32, so the split falls on a warp boundary
3: warps 0 to 2 run heavy()
8: any if statement makes every warp run both paths
1: only the warp containing thread 96
blocks.explain: Threads 0 to 95 are exactly warps 0, 1 and 2; threads 96 to 255 are warps 3 to 7. Every warp's 32 threads agree, so no warp has to run both paths. Divergence is a per-warp property, not a per-block one.

blocks.question: Code written for older GPUs reduces values within a warp through shared memory with no barriers, relying on the 32 threads moving in lockstep. On a compute capability 9.0 GPU it sometimes returns wrong sums. What is the fix?
options: Make the block size 32 so the warp is the whole block
Use __syncthreads() inside `if (threadIdx.x < 16)`
Add __syncwarp() between the dependent shared memory steps
Nothing can be done; warp-level reductions are unsupported after Volta
blocks.explain: Since compute capability 7.0, threads of a warp can diverge and reconverge at sub-warp granularity, so lockstep is not guaranteed. The guide says to make such code explicit with __syncwarp(). Calling __syncthreads() under a condition that only some threads satisfy is itself undefined behavior (next lesson).

lessons.title: Cooperating inside a block: shared memory, barriers and clusters

blocks.md:
Threads of one block can cooperate because they live on the same SM. Two tools make that possible:

- **Shared memory**: an on-chip scratchpad declared with `__shared__`, visible to all threads of the block and alive for the block's lifetime. It is carved out of the same physical storage as the L1 cache and has much higher bandwidth and lower latency than global memory.
- **`__syncthreads()`**: a block-wide barrier. No thread passes it until every non-exited thread of the block has reached it, and all memory writes before the barrier are visible to all participating threads after it.

blocks.caption: Adapted from the CUDA guide's __syncthreads example: each thread stages one value, then thread 0 sums the block.

blocks.prompt: Delete the `__syncthreads()` line. Thread 0 is in warp 0, which may run well ahead of warps 1 to 3. What can thread 0 read?
blocks.reveal: Some of `s[32..127]` may not have been written yet, so thread 0 can add stale or garbage values. The bug is timing dependent: it may pass every test on one GPU and fail on another. Shared memory is not initialized for you.

blocks.title: A data race in shared memory (8-thread toy block)

scenes.caption: Simplified to 8 threads in 2 groups of 4 (think: two warps). Shared memory starts with unknown contents.
No barrier: the first group has stored its values, the second has not, and thread 0 already starts summing. It reads 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 plus four garbage values.
With __syncthreads(): nobody passes the barrier until all 8 stores are done, so thread 0 reads every value and gets 36.

blocks.title: Warps of one 128-thread block meeting at __syncthreads()

scenes.caption: Illustrative timings: the 4 warps finish their stores at different times because the scheduler interleaves them.
Early warps wait at the barrier (muted) until the last warp arrives at step 7. Only then does thread 0 in warp 0 start the sum.
Bug: the barrier sits inside `if (threadIdx.x < 64)`. Warps 2 and 3 never reach it, so warps 0 and 1 may wait forever. The guide calls this undefined behavior: it may hang or misbehave.

blocks.md: `__syncthreads()` may appear in conditional code only if the condition evaluates the same way for every thread in the block. Otherwise execution may hang or produce unintended side effects. Hoist the barrier out of the branch.

**Thread block clusters.** Compute capability 9.0 (Hopper) added an optional level between block and grid. A **cluster** groups adjacent blocks of the grid (in 1, 2 or 3 dimensions) and guarantees they are scheduled *at the same time* on SMs of one **GPC** (graphics processing cluster, a group of SMs). That co-scheduling is what makes cross-block cooperation safe inside a cluster:

- `cluster.sync()` (Cooperative Groups) is a barrier across all blocks of the cluster.
- **Distributed shared memory**: a block can read, write and do atomics on the shared memory of other blocks in its cluster, via `cluster.map_shared_rank()`.

The maximum *portable* cluster size is 8 blocks; H100 allows 16 with an explicit non-portable opt-in. Clusters do not change the grid's dimensions or block indices.

blocks.caption: Cluster syntax from the guide's language extensions chapter; sizes can also be set at runtime with cudaLaunchKernelEx.

blocks.title: A grid of 4 blocks launched as 2 clusters of 2

scenes.caption: Same grid as before: 4 blocks. Specifying a cluster size of 2 groups adjacent blocks 0 and 1, and 2 and 3. Block indices are unchanged.
Each cluster's blocks are launched together on SMs of a single GPC, so they are guaranteed to be running at the same time.
Inside a cluster, blocks can access each other's shared memory and meet at cluster.sync(). Across clusters (block 1 and block 2) the old rule still holds: no ordering, no waiting.

blocks.question: A kernel uses a 48 KB shared-memory tile and `__syncthreads()`. A teammate proposes having block 7 read the tile that block 3 just loaded, to save a global memory read. When is that allowed?
options: Always: shared memory is shared by the whole grid
Never, under any launch configuration
Only if blocks 3 and 7 are in the same thread block cluster, using distributed shared memory and cluster.sync() on compute capability 9.0 or later
Only if both blocks call __syncthreads() first
blocks.explain: Ordinary shared memory is private to one block. Clusters (CC 9.0+) let blocks in the same cluster map each other's shared memory, because the cluster's blocks are co-scheduled. With a portable cluster size of at most 8, blocks 3 and 7 would need a cluster shape that contains both, which a 1D cluster of 8 starting at block 0 does. __syncthreads() never reaches across blocks.

blocks.question: Which barrier placement is valid?
options: `if (blockIdx.x % 2 == 0) { __syncthreads(); }`
`if (threadIdx.x % 2 == 0) { __syncthreads(); }`
`if (threadIdx.x < 64) { __syncthreads(); }`
`for (int k = 0; k < threadIdx.x; ++k) __syncthreads();`
blocks.explain: blockIdx.x is the same for every thread in a block, so the condition is uniform across the block and either all of its threads reach the barrier or none do. The other three depend on threadIdx, so some threads of the block skip or repeat the barrier: undefined behavior.

lessons.title: Occupancy: how many warps fit on an SM at once

blocks.md:
An SM hides the latency of a slow load by switching to another warp that is ready: every resident warp keeps its registers and program counter on chip, so switching costs nothing. That only works if enough warps are **resident** (assigned to the SM at the same time).

**Occupancy** is the ratio of active warps on an SM to the maximum it can hold. It is capped by several per-SM budgets, and whichever runs out first decides how many blocks fit.

blocks.caption: b = threads per block, r = registers per thread, s = shared memory per block. Occupancy = blocks x warps per block / 64. Simplified: ignores allocation granularity.

blocks.prompt: 256-thread blocks, 32 registers per thread, no shared memory. Then the compiler grows the kernel to 64 registers per thread. What happens to occupancy?
blocks.reveal: At 32 registers a block needs 256 x 32 = 8,192 registers, so 65,536 / 8,192 = 8 blocks fit: 8 x 8 = 64 warps, **100%**. At 64 registers a block needs 16,384, so only 4 blocks fit: 32 warps, **50%**. The Best Practices Guide's rule of thumb follows: 65,536 / 2,048 = 32 registers per thread is the most you can use at full occupancy.

blocks.title: Occupancy on a compute capability 9.0 SM (simplified model)

scenes.caption: Baseline: 8 blocks of 8 warps fill all 64 warp slots. Registers (8 blocks) and the warp limit (8 blocks) bind at the same time.
Doubling registers to 64 halves the blocks that fit (4), so 32 of 64 warps: 50%. Registers are allocated per block, all at once.
48 KB of shared memory per block (49 KB with the reserved 1 KB): 228 / 49 rounds down to 4 blocks, 50%. Shared memory is the binding budget here.
Tiny blocks of 32 threads: the 32-blocks-per-SM limit binds first, giving 32 warps, 50%, even though registers would allow far more.
Huge blocks are coarse: 1024 threads x 40 registers = 40,960 registers, so only 1 block (32 warps) fits. With 256-thread blocks at 40 registers, 6 blocks fit: 48 warps, 75%.

blocks.title: Occupancy vs registers per thread (compute capability 9.0)

scenes.caption: 256-thread blocks, no shared memory: occupancy stays at 100% up to 32 registers per thread, then falls in steps as fewer whole blocks fit.
Add 48 KB of shared memory per block: the curve is capped at 50% (4 blocks) no matter how few registers you use.

1024-thread blocks: the steps are coarse. Above 32 registers occupancy drops straight to 50% because a second block no longer fits, and above 64 the block exceeds the 64 K registers an SM has, so it cannot launch at all.
64-thread blocks: finer steps, since the SM can top up with small blocks. Try other sizes; the model ignores register allocation granularity.

blocks.md: Real allocation is a bit coarser than this model. The Best Practices Guide notes that registers are rounded up to the nearest 256 per warp. Its compute capability 7.0 example: at 37 registers per thread, 128-thread blocks reach 75% occupancy (12 blocks) but 320-thread blocks only 63%, because just four of them fit. Use the occupancy calculator in Nsight Compute, `nvcc --ptxas-options=-v` to see register counts, or `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor` at runtime.

Higher occupancy is not automatically faster. Low occupancy hurts latency hiding, but past some point extra warps add nothing, and a lower-occupancy kernel can keep more data in registers and avoid spilling. Measure.

blocks.question: A kernel uses 256-thread blocks, 32 registers and 100 KB of shared memory per block on a compute capability 9.0 GPU. What limits occupancy, and to what?
options: Shared memory: 228 / (100 + 1) gives 2 blocks, 16 warps, 25%
Registers, to 100%
The 32-blocks-per-SM limit, to 50%
Threads per block: 256 is too small, so 12.5%
blocks.explain: Registers alone would allow 8 blocks, the warp limit 8, the block limit 32. Shared memory allows floor(228 / 101) = 2 blocks, which is the minimum: 2 x 8 = 16 warps of 64, 25%.

blocks.question: Profiling shows a memory-bound kernel at 50% occupancy. A teammate forces registers down from 64 to 32 per thread so it reaches 100%, and it gets slower. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Occupancy above 50% is impossible on compute capability 9.0
Capping registers made the compiler spill values to local memory, which lives in device memory, adding traffic that outweighed the extra warps
Higher occupancy always increases bank conflicts
The warp size changed to 64
blocks.explain: Register caps (-maxrregcount or __launch_bounds__) trade per-thread registers for more resident warps. If the kernel needs those registers it spills to local memory, which has global-memory latency and bandwidth. The guide warns that more occupancy does not always mean more performance.

lessons.title: The same model in Metal: threadgroups, SIMD-groups and dispatch

blocks.md: Apple's Metal Shading Language (MSL) uses the same three-level model under different names. A compute **kernel** runs over a 1D, 2D or 3D **grid** of threads; the grid is divided into **threadgroups** (CUDA's thread blocks), which share **threadgroup memory** (CUDA's shared memory); and a compute unit executes a threadgroup in smaller **SIMD-groups** (CUDA's warps, also called wavefronts on other GPUs).

blocks.title: CUDA terms and their Metal counterparts

scenes.caption: Left: CUDA. Right: Metal. The hierarchy maps one to one: a grid of threadgroups of threads.
The warp maps to the SIMD-group. CUDA fixes the warp at 32 on its GPUs; Metal tells you to query the width (threadExecutionWidth on the pipeline, threads_per_simdgroup in the kernel).
Cooperation inside a group: shared memory becomes the threadgroup address space, and the block barrier becomes threadgroup_barrier(mem_flags::mem_threadgroup).
Thread block clusters are a CUDA (compute capability 9.0+) feature; the MSL kernel attribute table lists no cluster level.

blocks.caption: Vector add in MSL, modeled on Apple's Performing Calculations on a GPU sample, which sizes the grid to exactly the array length.

blocks.md: **Two ways to dispatch.** `dispatchThreadgroups(_:threadsPerThreadgroup:)` is CUDA's model: you give a count of whole threadgroups, the grid is a multiple of the threadgroup size, and your kernel must bounds-check. `dispatchThreads(_:threadsPerThreadgroup:)` takes the *total* thread count; on GPUs that support **nonuniform threadgroups** (Apple4 family and later, per the feature set tables), Metal computes the number of threadgroups itself and makes the edge threadgroups smaller, so no thread lands outside the data. CUDA's `<<<>>>` has no such mode, which is why every CUDA kernel carries the `if (i < N)`.

blocks.prompt: An image of 1920 x 1080 pixels is processed with 32 x 16 threadgroups using dispatchThreadgroups. How many threadgroups are needed, and how many threads fall outside the image?
blocks.reveal: $\lceil 1920/32 \rceil = 60$ and $\lceil 1080/16 \rceil = 68$ (1080 / 16 = 67.5), so 60 x 68 = 4,080 threadgroups covering 1920 x 1088 threads. The extra 8 rows add 15,360 threads that must exit early. With dispatchThreads, Metal would instead make the bottom row of threadgroups only 8 threads tall.

blocks.title: Apple's example: one thread in a 16 x 16 grid of 8 x 4 threadgroups

scenes.caption: From Apple's Creating Threads and Threadgroups article: a 16 x 16 grid split into 2 x 4 threadgroups of 8 x 4 threads. Our thread sits at position (1, 2) in threadgroup (1, 2).
Grid position: x = 1 x 8 + 1 = 9, y = 2 x 4 + 2 = 10. This is what [[thread_position_in_grid]] delivers directly.
Linear index in the threadgroup: ly x Sx + lx = 2 x 8 + 1 = 17.
With a thread execution width of 16 (Apple's hypothetical example), the 32-thread group has 2 SIMD-groups of two rows each: index 17 is SIMD-group 1, lane 1.

blocks.md:
**Sizing a threadgroup.** Apple's guidance is to make the threadgroup a multiple of `threadExecutionWidth` and to stay within the pipeline's `maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup`, which can differ between two pipelines on the same device because it depends on the kernel's resource use. Apple's example: with a maximum of 512 and a width of 16, use a threadgroup of 16 x 32. The [feature set tables](https://developer.apple.com/metal/Metal-Feature-Set-Tables.pdf) list a theoretical maximum of 1024 threads and 32 KB of threadgroup memory per threadgroup on Apple4 and later GPUs.

Synchronization works like CUDA's: `threadgroup_barrier` must be reached by every thread of the threadgroup, and if it sits inside a conditional or loop, all threads must take the same path to it. `simdgroup_barrier` is the SIMD-group analog of `__syncwarp()`.

Portable rule for both APIs: never hard-code 32. In CUDA read `warpSize` when it matters; in Metal read `threadExecutionWidth` or `threads_per_simdgroup`. Write correct code that ignores the width, then tune block or threadgroup sizes as multiples of it.

blocks.question: You port a CUDA kernel to Metal and dispatch it with `dispatchThreads` for exactly N threads. The CUDA version had `if (i >= N) return;` at the top. What should you do with that check?
options: Keep it: Metal always rounds the grid up to whole threadgroups
It becomes redundant: with nonuniform threadgroups Metal launches exactly N threads, though keeping it is harmless
Replace it with threadgroup_barrier, which skips out-of-range threads
Change it to `if (i >= N * threadExecutionWidth)`
blocks.explain: dispatchThreads takes the total thread count and creates smaller edge threadgroups, so no thread position exceeds the data. Apple notes you do not need the position check in that case. With dispatchThreadgroups you would need it, just as in CUDA.

blocks.question: A Metal kernel assumes a SIMD-group is 32 wide and uses `thread_index_in_threadgroup / 32` to pick a SIMD-group's slot in threadgroup memory. What is the portable fix?
options: Nothing: every Metal GPU uses 32-wide SIMD-groups by specification
Use [[thread_position_in_grid]] / 32
Add threadgroup_barrier before the division
Use [[simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup]] (or divide by threads_per_simdgroup) instead of the constant 32
blocks.explain: MSL defines the SIMD-group width as a property you query (threads_per_simdgroup, or threadExecutionWidth on the host) and says the threadgroup is divided into SIMD-groups in an implementation-defined way. The built-in simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup gives the right answer on any GPU.
